content: The group of isometries in one, two, or three dimensions is defined as the collection of all transformations that preserve distances and under which the object remains invariant. These transformations are combined using composition as the group operation. This group is a subgroup of the isometry group of the corresponding space. In Euclidean geometry, symmetry groups are often studied, but the concept can also be extended to other contexts. The objects under consideration can include geometric figures, images, or patterns, such as wallpaper designs. These objects may also be functions of position with values in a set of colors or three-dimensional bodies, where physical composition might also be relevant. The isometry group of a space induces a group action on the objects within it. The symmetry group of an object is sometimes referred to as the full symmetry group to emphasize that it includes orientation-reversing isometries, such as reflections, glide reflections, and improper rotations, under which the object remains invariant. In contrast, the proper symmetry group of an object includes only orientation-preserving isometries, such as translations, rotations, and their compositions, which leave the object invariant. An object’s proper symmetry group is equal to its full symmetry group if and only if the object is chiral, meaning it has no orientation-reversing isometries under which it is invariant. Any symmetry group whose elements share a common fixed point can be represented as a subgroup of the orthogonal group O(n) by choosing the origin as the fixed point. This is true for all finite symmetry groups and for the symmetry groups of bounded figures. The proper symmetry group, in this case, is a subgroup of the special orthogonal group SO(n) and is also referred to as the rotation group of the object. Discrete symmetry groups can be categorized into three types: (1) finite point groups, which include only rotations, reflections, inversions, and rotoinversions and are finite subgroups of O(n); (2) infinite lattice groups, which include only translations; and (3) infinite space groups, which combine elements of the first two types and may also include additional transformations like screw axes and glide reflections. Continuous symmetry groups, on the other hand, include transformations such as rotations of arbitrarily small angles or translations of arbitrarily small distances. The group of all symmetries of a sphere, O(3), is an example of a continuous symmetry group, and such groups are generally studied as Lie groups. The classification of subgroups of the Euclidean group corresponds to a classification of symmetry groups. Two geometric figures are considered to have the same symmetry type if their symmetry groups are conjugate subgroups of the Euclidean group E(n), the isometry group of R^n. For example, the 17 wallpaper groups represent such classifications. When considering isometry groups, one may restrict attention to those where, for all points, the set of images under the isometries is topologically closed. This excludes, for instance, the group of translations by rational numbers in one dimension. A pattern with such a symmetry group would be non-drawable and homogeneous up to arbitrarily fine detail, without being truly homogeneous. In one dimension, the isometry groups where the set of images under the isometries is topologically closed include: The trivial group C1. Groups of two elements generated by a reflection in a point, isomorphic to C2. Infinite discrete groups generated by a translation, isomorphic to Z. Infinite discrete groups generated by a translation and a reflection in a point, isomorphic to the generalized dihedral group of Z, Dih(Z), also denoted by D∞ (a semidirect product of Z and C2). The group generated by all translations, isomorphic to R, which cannot be the symmetry group of a pattern as it would be homogeneous and hence could also be reflected. However, a uniform 1D vector field has this symmetry group. The group generated by all translations and reflections in points, isomorphic to the generalized dihedral group of R, Dih(R). In two dimensions, the isometry groups with a fixed point and topologically closed sets of images include: The special orthogonal group SO(2), consisting of all rotations about a fixed point, also called the circle group S1. This is the proper symmetry group of a circle and the continuous equivalent of Cn. The orthogonal group O(2), consisting of all rotations about a fixed point and reflections in any axis through that fixed point. This is the symmetry group of a circle and is also called Dih(S1), the generalized dihedral group of S1. For non-bounded figures, additional isometry groups can include translations. The closed ones are: The seven frieze groups. The 17 wallpaper groups. For each symmetry group in one dimension, the combination of all symmetries in that group in one direction and the group of all translations in the perpendicular direction. The same as above, but also including reflections in a line in the first direction. In three dimensions, the set of 3D point groups, up to conjugacy, consists of seven infinite series and seven separate ones. In crystallography, these groups are restricted to be compatible with the discrete translation symmetries of a crystal lattice. This restriction results in 32 crystallographic point groups (27 from the seven infinite series and five of the seven others). Continuous symmetry groups with a fixed point in three dimensions include those of: Cylindrical symmetry without a symmetry plane perpendicular to the axis, often applicable to objects like bottles. Cylindrical symmetry with a symmetry plane perpendicular to the axis. Spherical symmetry. For objects and scalar fields, cylindrical symmetry implies vertical planes of reflection and independence from the azimuthal angle φ. Reflective symmetry exists if and only if A_φ = 0. Spherical symmetry implies planes of reflection without such distinctions. Continuous symmetry groups without a fixed point include those with a screw axis, such as an infinite helix. In general, a symmetry group may be any kind of transformation group or automorphism group. Once the mathematical structure of interest is defined, the mappings that preserve the structure can be identified. Conversely, specifying the symmetry can define the structure or clarify what is meant by an invariant, providing a geometric language for discussion. This perspective aligns with the Erlangen program. For example, automorphism groups of certain finite geometry models are not symmetry groups in the usual sense, although they preserve symmetry by maintaining families of point-sets rather than the point-sets themselves. The group of automorphisms of space induces a group action on objects within it. In the case of a finite automorphism group of the whole space, its order is the product of the order of the symmetry group of the object and the number of isomorphic versions of the object. Examples include: Isometries of the Euclidean plane, where the object is a rectangle. There are infinitely many equivalence classes, each containing four isometries. A cube in Euclidean space with patterns or colors on its faces. The automorphisms of the space are the 48 isometries. If one face of the cube has a different color, the symmetry group of the object has eight isometries, with six equivalence classes of eight isometries each, corresponding to six isomorphic versions of the object.
